\begin{definition}[Frequency set decomposition equivalence]
\lean{FABL.frequencySplitEquiv}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p085-b004}
\label{FABL.frequencySplitEquiv}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedIndex}
For a finite coordinate set $J\subseteq\mathrm{Fin}(n)$, there is a bijection between
pairs $(A,B)$, where $A$ is a subset of $J$ and $B$ is a subset of the indices outside
$J$, and subsets of $\mathrm{Fin}(n)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Frequency split formula]
\lean{FABL.frequencySplitEquiv_apply}
\label{FABL.frequencySplitEquiv_apply}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedIndex, FABL.frequencySplitEquiv, FABL.liftFixedFrequency, FABL.liftFreeFrequency}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $J$ be a set of indices in $in$, and let $S$ be a
subset of $J$ and $T$ a subset of the indices outside $J$. Under the frequency split
equivalence, the pair $(S,T)$ corresponds to the union of $S$ and $T$, each viewed as a
subset of $in$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $f$ be a real-valued function on the
$n$-dimensional sign cube, and let $J$ be a subset of its coordinate set. For each
subset of $J$, form its restricted Fourier weight by summing the squared Fourier
coefficients over all frequencies obtained by adjoining a subset of the coordinates
outside $J$. The sum of these restricted Fourier weights over all subsets of $J$ equals
the sum of the squared Fourier coefficients of $f$ over all subsets of the full
coordinate set.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Restricted Fourier weight bound]
\lean{FABL.sum_restrictedFourierWeight_le_one}
\label{FABL.sum_restrictedFourierWeight_le_one}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.restrictedFourierWeight, FABL.restrictedFourierWeight_nonneg, FABL.sum_restrictedFourierWeight_eq_sum_sq_fourierCoeff, FABL.sum_sq_fourierCoeff_eq_one}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$ be a Boolean-valued
function, let $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and let $\mathcal A$ be any family of subsets
of $J$. For each $S\subseteq J$, sum the squared Fourier coefficients of $f$ over all
frequencies whose intersection with $J$ is $S$; the sum of these restricted weights over
$S\in\mathcal A$ is at most $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fourier coefficient bounded by restricted weight]
\lean{FABL.sq_fourierCoeff_le_restrictedFourierWeight}
\label{FABL.sq_fourierCoeff_le_restrictedFourierWeight}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedIndex, FABL.fixedFrequencyPart, FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.freeFrequencyPart, FABL.liftFixedFrequency, FABL.liftFreeFrequency, FABL.liftFreeFrequencyPart_union_liftFixedFrequencyPart, FABL.restrictedFourierWeight}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $f:\\{-1,1\\}^n\\to\\mathbb R$, and let $J$ and
$U$ be sets of coordinates. Let $S$ be a subset of $J$ equal to the part of $U$ lying in
$J$. Then the square of the Fourier coefficient of $f$ at $U$ is at most the restricted
Fourier weight of $f$ on $J$ at $S$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Full-coordinate Fourier weight]
\lean{FABL.restrictedFourierWeight_univ_freeFrequencyPart}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p084-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p085-b004
}
\label{FABL.restrictedFourierWeight_univ_freeFrequencyPart}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedIndex, FABL.fixedFrequencyPart, FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.freeFrequencyPart, FABL.liftFreeFrequencyPart_union_liftFixedFrequencyPart, FABL.restrictedFourierWeight}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f$ be a real-valued function on the sign cube
$\\{\\pm1\\}^n$, and let $U$ be a set of coordinates. When all coordinates are free, the
restricted Fourier weight indexed by the part of $U$ in the free coordinates equals the
square of the Fourier coefficient of $f$ at $U$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Prefix coordinate set]
\lean{FABL.prefixCoordinates}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p085-b004}
\label{FABL.prefixCoordinates}
\leanok
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the prefix coordinate set consists of the indices
$i\in\mathrm{Fin}(n)$ whose value is less than $k$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The empty zero-length prefix]
\lean{FABL.prefixCoordinates_zero}
\label{FABL.prefixCoordinates_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.prefixCoordinates}
\difficulty{3}
For every natural number $n$, the set of coordinates in $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ with index
less than zero is empty.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[A full prefix contains every coordinate]
\lean{FABL.prefixCoordinates_eq_univ}
\label{FABL.prefixCoordinates_eq_univ}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.prefixCoordinates}
\difficulty{3}
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$ with $n\le k$, the set of coordinates in
$\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ whose indices are less than $k$ is the full coordinate set.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers with $k<n$. The coordinates of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$
with index less than $k+1$ are the union of the coordinates with index less than $k$ and
the coordinate $k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Prefix of a frequency set]
\lean{FABL.prefixFrequency}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p085-b004}
\label{FABL.prefixFrequency}
\leanok
For a natural number $k$ and a finite set $U\subseteq\mathrm{Fin}(n)$, the prefix of $U$
consists of those $i\in U$ whose value is less than $k$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Empty zero prefix]
\lean{FABL.prefixFrequency_zero}
\label{FABL.prefixFrequency_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.prefixFrequency}
\difficulty{3}
For a natural number $n$ and a subset $U$ of $	ext{Fin}(n)$, the subset of elements of
$U$ whose indices are less than $0$ is empty.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[A sufficiently long prefix retains every frequency]
\lean{FABL.prefixFrequency_eq_self}
\label{FABL.prefixFrequency_eq_self}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.prefixFrequency}
\difficulty{3}
Let $U$ be a set of coordinates in $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, and let $k$ be a natural number
with $n\le k$. Filtering $U$ to retain only coordinates with index less than $k$ leaves
$U$ unchanged.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Prefix frequency lies in the prefix coordinates]
\lean{FABL.prefixFrequency_subset_prefixCoordinates}
\label{FABL.prefixFrequency_subset_prefixCoordinates}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.prefixCoordinates, FABL.prefixFrequency}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers, and let $U$ be a set of coordinates indexed by
$0,\ldots,n-1$. The coordinates in $U$ whose indices are less than $k$ are contained in
the set of all coordinates whose indices are less than $k$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{5}
Let $U$ be a set of coordinates in $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, and let $k<n$. The elements of
$U$ with index less than $k+1$ are obtained by adding coordinate $k$ to the elements
with index less than $k$ if $k\in U$; if $k\notin U$, the set is unchanged.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Free part of a prefix frequency set]
\lean{FABL.freeFrequencyPart_prefixFrequency}
\label{FABL.freeFrequencyPart_prefixFrequency}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.freeFrequencyPart, FABL.mem_freeFrequencyPart, FABL.prefixCoordinates, FABL.prefixFrequency}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers, and let $U$ be a subset of the coordinates
$\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. The part of the prefix of $U$ consisting of coordinates less than
$k$, restricted to the coordinates less than $k$, equals the part of $U$ on those
coordinates.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Lifting the restricted subset]
\lean{FABL.liftFreeFrequency_freeFrequencyPart_eq_of_subset}
\label{FABL.liftFreeFrequency_freeFrequencyPart_eq_of_subset}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.freeFrequencyPart, FABL.liftFreeFrequency, FABL.mem_freeFrequencyPart}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $J,S$ be subsets of $in n$ with $S\subseteq J$.
Regard the elements of $S$ as elements indexed by $J$ and then as elements of $in n$;
the resulting subset is exactly $S$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Injectivity of the free frequency part]
\lean{FABL.freeFrequencyPart_injOn_of_subsets}
\label{FABL.freeFrequencyPart_injOn_of_subsets}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.freeFrequencyPart, FABL.liftFreeFrequency, FABL.liftFreeFrequency_freeFrequencyPart_eq_of_subset}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $J$ be a subset of the coordinates $\\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$,
and let $\mathcal A$ be a finite family of coordinate subsets, each contained in $J$.
The map sending each $U\in\mathcal A$ to its part inside $J$ is injective on $\mathcal
A$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Goldreich–Levin threshold range]
\lean{FABL.GoldreichLevinThreshold}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p083-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p090-b005
}
\label{FABL.GoldreichLevinThreshold}
\leanok
The Goldreich–Levin threshold range is the set of rational numbers $\tau$ satisfying
$0<\tau\leq 1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Goldreich–Levin active cap]
\lean{FABL.goldreichLevinActiveCap}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p083-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p085-b003
}
\label{FABL.goldreichLevinActiveCap}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.GoldreichLevinThreshold}
For a rational threshold $\tau$ with $0<\tau\leq1$, the active cap is the least natural
number greater than or equal to $4/\tau^{2}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Bound on qualifying Fourier prefixes]
\lean{FABL.card_prefixes_le_goldreichLevinActiveCap}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p085-b003}
\label{FABL.card_prefixes_le_goldreichLevinActiveCap}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.GoldreichLevinThreshold, FABL.card_prefixes_mul_minWeight_le_one, FABL.freeFrequencyPart, FABL.goldreichLevinActiveCap, FABL.restrictedFourierWeight}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f$ be a function from the Boolean cube $\{-1,1\}^n$
to $\{-1,1\}$, let $J$ be a set of coordinates, and let $\mathcal A$ be a family of
subsets of the coordinates. Choose a rational threshold $\tau$ with $0<\tau\le 1$. If
each $S\in\mathcal A$ is contained in $J$, and its restricted Fourier weight on $J$ is
at least $\tau^2/4$, then $\mathcal A$ has cardinality at most $\lceil
4/\tau^2\rceil$.
\end{theorem}
